                   PREFACE


     Reading is the cornerstone of learning, yet it remains one of
the most pressing challenges in education today. In response, the
Division of Bukidnon proudly introduces Bukidnon’s Unified
Literacy and Intervention Gateway (BULIG) — a transformative
innovation designed  to improve  learners’ reading  ability and
empower every child to succeed.

   BULIG is more than a program; it is a unified movement for
literacy, built on collaboration, evidence-based strategies, and a
deep commitment to equity in education. This initiative bridges
gaps in reading proficiency by providing targeted interventions,
innovative approaches, and sustainable support systems that
cater to the diverse needs of learners across the division.

    Anchored on this vision, the Division of Bukidnon integrates
the ARAL Program (Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning),
a national initiative focused on learning recovery and remediation.
ARAL provides structured and learner-centered interventions for
those struggling with foundational skills in reading and numeracy.
By complementing BULIG’s  mission, ARAL  strengthens  the
division’s  comprehensive  approach  to  literacy,  ensuring  that
learners overcome difficulties and gain the confidence to succeed
academically. Together, these programs create a powerful synergy
that accelerates learning recovery and builds a strong foundation
for lifelong learning.

    Through BULIG, we envision classrooms where every
learner reads with confidence. Comprehends with clarity, and
learns with purpose. This gateway opens  opportunities  for
lifelong learning, ensuring that no child is left behind in the
journey toward academic excellence and personal growth.

     Together, let us make literacy not just a goal, but a reality for
all.

Learning Competency: Asking Questions

Instructions: Things you should know:

    •  Number of Players: 2-10

    •  Setup: Choose 1 player to be “it,” and have them think of a secret
      person, place or thing.

    •  Object of the game: Other players attempt to guess the secret person,
      place, or thing, but they only get 20 questions to do so.

30


"This game works best with a small to medium-sized group of people, so that
everyone gets a chance to ask a question. Choose a random player to be “it.”
This could be the youngest player in the group, the player who’s had the most
recent birthday, or something silly, like who can eat a piece of pizza the
fastest.

Question 1





Think of a person, place, or thing for other players to guess if you’re “it. ”Think
of someone or something that you know enough about to answer some basic
questions about, and keep  it a secret! If you choose a person, they can be
living, deceased, or even fictional. Make sure you choose a person, place, or
thing that most people in your group know about.

    •  For example, your item could be “Manny Pacquiao,” since he is famous
     enough that most people will be able to make guesses about him. You
      could also choose something like your town, Philippines, or even clouds
      or the sun.

    •  Avoid items like “my mom” or “my dog” unless you are with your siblings
      or best friends, since the players might not know enough about them
      to guess.





Question 2




Ask yes-or-no questions if you're not "it. "If you’re not “it,” your goal is to figure
out what the “it” person is thinking of by asking questions to narrow down
the possibilities. Try using a fairly general opening question that can be
answered with “yes” or “no” to narrow down your options.

31


For example:
    •   “Is it alive?”
    •  “Is it an object?”
    •   “Is it fictional?”
    •  “Is it bigger than a toaster?
Question 3





Take turns asking more specific yes-or-no questions to narrow it down. You
can ask questions in any order that you’d like, but make sure each player
gets to ask at least 1 question.  If a player asks a question that can’t be
answered with “yes” or “no,” ask them to rephrase it so that it can be, since
the person who’s “it” can only say “yes” or “no.”

    •  For example, a player couldn’t ask, “How old are they?” or “What do
      they look like?” They could ask, “Are they older than 50?” or, “Do they
     have blonde hair?”

Think about the questions that have already been asked before you ask new
questions. For example, you could go from "Is it a person?" to "Is it a man?"
to "Are they alive?" to "Do they live in the Philippines?"

Play until you reach 10 questions or someone guesses the right answer.
Become the next “it” person if you guess the correct answer. The person who
guesses the right answer is next to be “it,” and they think up their own secret
person, place, or thing. If no one guessed the person, place, or thing at all,
whoever wants to go next can have a turn. Keep the game going until everyone
has had a chance to be “it.”

    •   If someone guesses correctly but they’ve already been “it,” let someone
      else have a turn instead. Giving everyone a turn makes the game more
      inclusive and lets everybody have some fun!

Additional Intervention Material DESCRIBE and DRAW

Instructions: 1. Show a picture. The picture might be a page from a
storybook that the children are familiar with, or a picture like one of these.





2. Ask children what they see. “What do you see in the pictures?” or “What do
you notice?” Learners’ answers may vary. Accept their responses. We want to
get children to begin to describe what they see in their own words.

    •   “I see a house.”
    •   “I see a door.”
    •   “I see a girl flying.”
    •   “I see a weird tree.”
    •   “I see squares.”

3. Take the children's lead and respond to their ideas by asking follow-up
questions.

    •  "Where do you see the squares? Where do you see the tree?"
    •  "Can you tell me more about the         ?"
    •  "What do you notice about what’s in the back corner?"
    •  "How do you know that this is a triangle? Are those both triangles?"

4. Ask students to draw what they see.

    •  Keep the picture available; this is not a memory task.
    •  This is not a tracing task either. We are asking children to draw what
     they see. (Expect a wide variety!)
    •  Children often begin by drawing portions of the picture (just the tree,
       just the oval for the body of the tree, etc.)

33


5. Move around and check in with them as they are drawing. You can ask
questions based on what they drew to get them to add detail to their drawing.
It  is important to remember  that the children should not think  that the
drawing has to look exactly like the picture. “You draw what YOU see.” (You
might want to remind children that what they see might be different from
what someone else sees.)

6. As children finish, ask them to tell you about what they drew. Older
children could describe their own drawing to a partner, and vice versa. After
discussion, children should go back and add detail to their own drawing.

7. Consider sharing a couple of examples of children's drawings and ask the
child to describe to the class what they drew. Let other children add what they
see. Use this as an opportunity to highlight one idea you want to engage the
group in (perhaps noticing a particular shape, or using specific language such
as above or below, or describing where an object is in relation to other
objects).

Additional Intervention Material STORY CHAIN

Learning Competency: Retelling a short story.

Instructions: A Story Chain is a simple method of passing a story around the
class, giving each student plenty of practice in storytelling.

Prepare a Story

Choose short stories that can be told in 1-3 minutes. You may consider these
sample stories suggested.

Running the Activity

Let the pupils come together in pairs. Each pair is given a short picture story.
Give them time to work through it by making their own story about the
pictures. At the teachers signal, students A will tell the story to student B.
Break up the pair and each child gets a new partner. They take turns in
retelling the story they heard from their first partners to the new partner.

You can do this several times. At the end you get individuals from the class
to recite the last story they heard and then compare it with the original, see if
it has improved in the storytelling, see what facts have changed completely
and maybe see if the original storyteller can actually recognize their story!


Sample stories:

Story 1 Mia and the Shiny Stone

I have a cat named Mia. It is an orange cat. While playing in the garden, Mia
found a shiny blue stone. She found it under the red rose buds. The stone
was so smooth and bright that Mia held it gently in her paws. Suddenly, the
stone made a tiny ding sound! Mia’s ears perked up.

Story 2 Pip the Rabbit and the Wobbly Carrot

My father bought me a rabbit. I named him Pip. Pip, is a white rabbit. It dug
up a purple carrot. It felt soft and wobbly in his teeth. Pip was about to take
a bite but the carrot jiggled on its own!

Story 3 Lila the Bird’s Lost Song

My sister Jessa has a blue bird that forgot how to sing. It did not cheep. No
trills, no sound, just silence. The bird found a tiny paper note under a tree

Additional Intervention Material PICTURE TALK

Picture  talk  activities  are  engaging  ways  to  enhance  children's
communication   skills,  imagination,  and  comprehension  through
discussions bas ed on images.

What is a Picture Talk Activity?

A picture talk activity involves using images to spark discussions among
children. This method encourages kids to observe, analyze, and express their
thoughts about  the  pictures,  fostering  their communication and  literacy
skills.  It can be adapted to various topics, making  it a versatile tool for
learning.

Steps to Create Picture Talk Activities

   1. Choose a Topic: Select a theme that interests the children, such as
      nature, family, or sports. This helps to engage them more effectively.

   2. Select a Picture: Find a picture that aligns with the chosen topic. It
      should be  visually  stimulating and  rich  in  details  to  encourage
      discussion.

   3. Project the Image: Display the picture on a screen or print it out for
      the children to see. This allows everyone to focus on the same visual
      stimulus.
